newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada dollar scenario now less rosy - economists.
newsitem.headline: Canada dollar scenario now less rosy - economists.

text.p: Economists, who only three months ago were calling for an US$0.80 (C$1.250) Canadian dollar by the end of 1997, are now hedging their bets.
The dollar, which entered 1997 as one of the currencies favored to outperform among G7 nations, looks to be suffering from a slight case of the mid-winter blues.

A recent downdraft has shaved 1.2 percent off the Canadian currency's value against the U.S. dollar in the past two months. Now trading at C$1.3632 (US$0.7335), it sank last week to C$1.3713 (US$0.7292) -- its second lowest rate this year.
"There is a lot more caution on the (Canadian) dollar. We've shifted our outlook to neutral," said Doug Porter, senior economist with Nesbitt Burns.
The sudden slide of the Canadian currency flies in the face of predictions by 21 Canadian and U.S. economists polled by Reuters at the beginning of the year.
At that time, an overwhelming majority were strongly bullish on the Canadian dollar.

But European, Asian and U.S. investors have been spooked by a spate of bad economic news out of Canada, the specter of another Quebec sovereignty referendum and the possible widening of spreads between U.S. and Canadian interest rates.
Traders said this volatile economic cocktail could produce dizzy spells for the Canadian dollar in 1997.
"The best we're going to see this year is US$0.75 (C$1.333), probably sometime in the third quarter," said Stephen Wateridge, managing director of corporate foreign exchange with CIBC Wood Gundy.
Last week, Statistics Canada, the federal government's statistical agency, reported that Canadian employment growth in January declined by 18,000 jobs.
The unexpected drop set off an immediate Canada dollar selling flurry and a flight to the safer haven of the U.S. dollar.
Canada dollar selling was spurred by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's recent comments that a hike in U.S. interest rates to combat creeping U.S. inflation was possible.
"It is now clear that there will be a divergence between U.S. and Canada monetary policy in the next six months," Porter said.
He added it was unlikely that the Bank of Canada would follow a Fed move to raise interest rates, making some short-term weakening of the Canadian dollar inevitable.
Currency traders also continue to fret about rumors of an impending provincial election and snap sovereignty referendum in the French-speaking province of Quebec.

"Quebec is the grey cloud on the horizon which will continue to haunt Canada and the (Canadian) dollar," Wateridge said. "When international players get wind of a resurgence in separatism, they tend to liquidate their Canada positions."
Despite its relative weakness against the U.S. dollar, Canada's dollar has fared well against other major currencies, including the German mark and Japanese yen.
Since January 1, it has risen to 1.241 marks from 1.121 marks and jumped to 89.70 yen from 84 yen.
